title: LDDS: cheap long distance from Mississippi
what: LDDS, a long-distance telephone company from Jackson, Mississippi, resells calls over AT&T's network at a discount to small businesses. Founded in 1983 in a Hattiesburg coffee shop and run since 1985 by Bernard Ebbers, a former basketball coach and motel owner, it grows by buying small regional rivals and paying with its own shares; in 1989 it merged with Advantage Companies.
why: Listing beat. Growth by acquisition paid in stock works only while the stock keeps rising; that dependence is the thread of the whole arc.

title: LDDS shares have quadrupled in eighteen months
what: Shares of LDDS have roughly quadrupled since the start of 1990 as the company keeps buying smaller long-distance companies.
why: The early run (+30% in June 1990, +31% in January 1991, +26% in July 1991) has no confirmed single cause; the price data for 1990-92 is also unverified (see Unexplained moves).

title: LDDS outbids AT&T and Sprint for a rival
what: LDDS has bought Advanced Telecommunications Corporation for about $720 million, outbidding the much larger Sprint and AT&T. The deal makes LDDS a substantially bigger player in long distance.
why: The first big deal. Wikipedia dates it to 1992 without a month; the beat is placed at the year end and the month should be checked before use.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCI_Inc. (read 2026-10-03, citing New York Times, 1 May 2002)

title: LDDS merges with Metromedia's and Resurgens' phone businesses
what: LDDS has combined with Metromedia Communications and Resurgens Communications Group, making it a national long-distance carrier with Bernard Ebbers as chief executive. Billionaire John Kluge, owner of Metromedia, becomes a major shareholder. Sales are on course for about $1.1 billion this year.
why: The three-way merger made LDDS a national carrier. The 1993 date is from the LA Times; the month is not confirmed.

title: LDDS becomes WorldCom and buys WilTel's network
what: At its annual meeting LDDS renamed itself WorldCom. It is buying WilTel Network Services of Tulsa, Oklahoma, a long-distance network operator, for $2.5 billion in cash. WorldCom lost nearly $150 million in 1994 because of the IDB merger, on revenue that doubled to $2.2 billion.
why: From discount reseller to network owner. Salomon Brothers' telecom analyst Jack Grubman started covering the stock this month with a 'buy'.

title: WorldCom to take over MCI for $37 billion
what: WorldCom agreed to buy MCI Communications, the second-largest U.S. long-distance company and more than three times WorldCom's size, for about $37 billion in stock, the largest takeover in history. MCI had been about to merge with British Telecom.
why: The deal that made WorldCom a giant, paid for entirely with its own highly valued shares.

title: Regulators kill the Sprint deal
what: WorldCom and Sprint called off their merger on 13 July after the U.S. Justice Department and the European Union said they would block it, arguing it would limit competition in long distance and put too much of the internet under one company.
why: The end of growth by acquisition. By later accounts the accounting fraud began modestly in mid-1999 and accelerated from 2001, as management tried to keep reported earnings on track.

title: WorldCom splits itself in two and writes off $685 million
what: On 1 November WorldCom announced it would split its business into two tracking stocks: WorldCom group for data, internet and business customers, and MCI group for the shrinking consumer long-distance business, which will pay a dividend. It has taken a $685 million third-quarter charge for customers that cannot pay, as many small telecom companies go bankrupt, and its growth is slowing. A filing on 14 November disclosed that WorldCom had lent chief executive Bernard Ebbers money and guaranteed his loans so he would not have to sell shares to meet margin calls.
why: Three warning signs in one month: slowing growth, bad debts from a collapsing customer base, and a board lending the boss money to prop up his shareholding. The shares fell 37%.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723527/000091205701505916/a2043540z10-k405.txt (WorldCom 10-K for 2000, describing the 1 November announcement and the third-quarter charge; read 2026-10-03); http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/money/industries/telecom/2002-11-05-ebbers-loans-timeline_x.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Surprise rate cut lifts beaten-down telecom shares
what: The Federal Reserve cut interest rates by half a percentage point on 3 January, saying the economy was weakening. Shares that had fallen hardest in 2000, telecoms among them, rebounded; WorldCom's rose by half in January after losing more than half in the autumn.
why: A bear-market rally: the rebound was gone by the summer.

title: WorldCom cuts 6,000 jobs
what: WorldCom is laying off about 6,000 workers across the country.
why: Cost cuts as revenue growth stalled; behind the scenes, the improper capitalisation of line costs started in 2001.

title: WorldCom's two tracking stocks begin trading
what: Shareholders approved the split, and from 8 June each WorldCom share became one share of WorldCom group stock plus 1/25 of a share of MCI group stock, which will pay a quarterly dividend of 60 cents. WorldCom group revenues grew 12% in the first quarter. In May it raised billions of dollars by selling bonds through a syndicate led by Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney.
why: The game follows the WorldCom group share; the small MCI group distribution is not added back. The bonds sold in May 2001 and May 2002 came to about $17 billion, money the bondholders largely lost.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723527/000089375001500127/exh99_1.txt (WorldCom press release, 7 June 2001; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723527/000100547701500032/ex99-1.txt (26 April 2001; read 2026-10-03); https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/wallstreet/wcom/cron.html (read 2026-10-03)

title: Global Crossing goes bankrupt; telecom shares slump
what: Global Crossing, which built undersea fibre-optic cables, filed for bankruptcy in January with debts of $12.4 billion, one of the largest bankruptcies ever. Coming weeks after Enron's collapse, it deepened fears about debt and accounting at telecom companies, and WorldCom's shares fell 29% in the month.
why: Contagion from Enron and the telecom bust; investors started to ask how WorldCom's profits could hold up when its customers and rivals were failing.

title: WorldCom paid $199 million to cover its chief's margin loans
what: WorldCom disclosed on 7 February that, after the fall in its shares, it had paid about $198.7 million to Bank of America under its guarantee of loans to chief executive Bernard Ebbers, and had lent him another $142 million, all secured by his WorldCom shares. Ebbers used the money to meet calls on loans backed by his stock, taken out for private businesses. The same day the company felt it had to reaffirm the MCI group's 60-cent dividend.
why: The clearest public warning: shareholders' money was being used to stop the chief executive's share sales. The stock fell another quarter.

title: WorldCom adopts a takeover defence
what: WorldCom's board adopted a shareholder rights plan on 8 March to discourage what it called opportunistic, undervalued takeover bids, saying it knew of no bid. Its annual report, filed on 13 March, put Ebbers' loans from the company at $144.3 million.
why: A board protecting a falling stock from buyers rather than asking why it was falling.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723527/000100547702001225/ex99.txt (WorldCom press release, 8 March 2002; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723527/000100547702001226/d02-36461.txt (10-K for 2001; read 2026-10-03)

title: Ebbers resigns as WorldCom's shares collapse
what: Bernard Ebbers resigned as chief executive on 30 April after the board, which had lost patience with his loans, demanded he go; John Sidgmore, former head of UUNet, replaces him. The SEC is investigating WorldCom's accounting. On 22 April Salomon Smith Barney analyst Jack Grubman, long WorldCom's biggest supporter, cut his rating to 'neutral'. The shares fell 63% in April, to below $3.
why: The founder gone, the regulator in, the cheerleader silent. Grubman had kept a 'buy' while the stock fell over 90% from its 1999 peak.

title: WorldCom cut to junk; scraps the MCI dividend
what: The rating agencies have cut WorldCom's debt to junk (Moody's Ba2, Standard & Poor's BB), and the company plans to draw $2.65 billion from a bank credit line while it negotiates new, secured loans. It expects to write off $15-20 billion of goodwill from past acquisitions, has replaced Arthur Andersen as auditor with KPMG, has rolled Bernard Ebbers' debts to the company into a single $408 million note, and on 21 May said it would scrap the MCI tracking stock and its dividend to save $284 million a year.
why: A company that needs its banks and cuts its dividend is short of cash; the new auditor's work led straight to the fraud.

title: WorldCom admits a $3.8 billion accounting fraud
what: WorldCom said on 25 June that it had hidden $3.8 billion of ordinary expenses over five quarters by booking them as investments, turning losses into profits; it fired finance chief Scott Sullivan and must restate its results for 2001 and 2002. The SEC charged the company with fraud the next day. Earlier in the month WorldCom announced 17,000 job cuts; it has about $30 billion of debt.
why: The largest accounting fraud uncovered in the United States until then, found by the company's own internal auditors. The fraud later grew to about $11 billion.

title: WorldCom files for bankruptcy, the largest in U.S. history
what: WorldCom filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 21 July, the largest filing in U.S. history, overtaking Enron. Days earlier, Bernard Ebbers told a congressional committee he had nothing to hide and then refused to answer questions, citing his right not to incriminate himself. The shares are close to worthless.
why: The exit. Shareholders were wiped out; Ebbers was later sentenced to 25 years in prison, and Citigroup paid $2.65 billion to settle claims over the WorldCom shares and bonds it sold.
